primaryEvidence.title: Fisheries and Oceans Canada, 2005 species account
primaryEvidence.finding: Adult pigmentation varies with age; the belly is paler than the back. The back lacks a dorsal fin. The left tooth usually erupts in males, with exceptional tooth states.
primaryEvidence.application: Retain the finless supplied exterior and select an adult dorsal/ventral pigment field. Offer usual left and rare paired eruption. Historical legal status and longevity estimates are not adopted.

primaryEvidence.title: Natural History Museum, two-tusked collection specimen
primaryEvidence.read: Collection account and complete two-tusk skull photograph.
primaryEvidence.finding: The usual erupted tooth is on the left upper jaw, with a leftward spiral; rare animals also erupt the right tooth.
primaryEvidence.application: Use the supplied separate left and right tusks. No prevalence estimate or measured socket/helix fit. Museum image remains a private reference.

primaryEvidence.title: Tervo et al. 2021, Hunting by the Stroke
primaryEvidence.read: Methods, body posture/stroke detection, results and Tables 2/4; no supplementary video.
primaryEvidence.finding: The study instrumented 13 narwhals; 11 had suitable 100-Hz acceleration records. Table 2 gives a surface median of 24 strokes/min. Stroking and gliding differ with dive context; supine posture occurs. The detector achieved 81% correct detection in its checked subset.
primaryEvidence.application: Use 0.4 Hz as cohort context only. Posterior amplitude, roll transition and 12-second envelope are authored. The quiet display segment is not a measured natural glide; the paper’s continuous-glide analysis uses bouts of at least 20 seconds. No dive, oxygen, pressure or energetic model.

primaryEvidence.title: O’Corry-Crowe et al. 2025, tusk use in foraging, exploration and play
primaryEvidence.read: Publisher methods/results and complete schematic Figures 2A–H and 3A–F; no supplementary video.
primaryEvidence.finding: UAV observations show pursuit, tusk contact/manipulation, fish escape, gull interactions and likely exploratory play. Tusk contact does not invariably establish capture.
primaryEvidence.application: A restrained closed-mouth orientation study carries the upper teeth rigidly with the body. No spearing, chewing, fish collision, successful capture, jaw intake or suction calculation is depicted.

suppliedPhotos.use: Qualitative adult shape, pigmentation and tusk-state comparison. Rendered/illustrative-looking references are not treated as observations or measurements. No source/individual identity is asserted from these images.

physiology: Species context informs the exterior and limits. There is no tissue, acoustic, sensory, oxygen, pressure, energetic or hydrodynamic solver.
